summary: For every cell of a binary matrix return its distance (in edge steps) to the nearest 0.
mainInsight: Run one BFS that starts from every 0 at once. BFS reaches cells in order of distance, so the first time a 1-cell is reached is via its nearest 0, and its distance is its parent's distance + 1.
invariant: Cells are dequeued in non-decreasing distance, and a cell's distance is final the moment it is first enqueued.

approaches.name: BFS from each 1-cell
approaches.summary: For every 1, BFS until a 0 is found.

approaches.name: Multi-source BFS from all zeros
approaches.summary: Enqueue all zeros at distance 0; expand level by level.

approaches.name: Two-pass DP
approaches.summary: Top-left to bottom-right taking min(up, left) + 1, then bottom-right to top-left with down/right.
weaknesses: Needs the argument why two passes suffice

personalSolution.approach: Multi-source BFS from all zeros, writing distances into mat and tracking a seen set
personalSolution.notes: Optimal. The level loop (k = len(queue)) is not needed since distances come from the parent. Mutating the input is fine here but worth mentioning.

commonMistakes: Using DFS, which does not visit cells in distance order.
One DP pass only (up and left), which misses zeros below or to the right.
Not marking cells when enqueued, so they are processed several times.
edgeCases: Single 0 in a corner of a large matrix.

promptVariants: Why start the BFS from the zeros instead of from the ones?
What does reversing the search direction (0s -> 1s) buy?
options: One BFS labels every cell, not one BFS per cell
Zeros are fewer than ones, so the queue is smaller
BFS from ones would give wrong distances
Starting from zeros avoids needing a visited check
cards.answer: One BFS labels every cell, not one BFS per cell
cards.explanation: All zeros are sources at distance 0. The multi-source BFS reaches every cell first from its nearest zero, so a single O(m * n) traversal labels the whole matrix.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Zeros are fewer than ones, so the queue: Nothing guarantees fewer zeros; the gain is one search instead of many.
incorrectOptionExplanations.BFS from ones would give wrong distances: Per-cell BFS is correct, just repeated.
incorrectOptionExplanations.Starting from zeros avoids needing a vis: You still must mark cells to avoid re-enqueueing.

cards.explanation: The only 0 is at row 2. Row 1 and row 3 are one step away and row 0 is two steps away.

incorrectOptionExplanations.[[1], [1], [0], [1]]: That is the input unchanged; row 0 is two steps from the 0.
incorrectOptionExplanations.[[3], [2], [0], [1]]: Off by one: row 1 touches the 0 directly.

promptVariants: How does the two-pass DP work, and why are two passes enough?
Describe the DP alternative to BFS.
cards.answer: Pass 1 (top-left to bottom-right): dist = 0 for zeros, else min(up, left) + 1. Pass 2 (bottom-right to top-left): dist = min(dist, down + 1, right + 1). Any shortest path to the nearest 0 can be split into moves that go up/left and moves that go down/right, and the two sweeps propagate each kind. O(m * n) time and no queue.
keyPoints: Forward pass uses up and left
Backward pass uses down and right
Shortest grid path combines the two directions
Same O(m * n) time, no queue
cards.explanation: Good to mention as an equally optimal answer; BFS is easier to justify on the spot.

promptVariants: In the canonical code, why is a cell's distance set when it is enqueued rather than when popped?
What does writing dist[nr][nc] at enqueue time guarantee?
options: Each cell is enqueued once, at its nearest distance
Distances set at pop time would always be off by one
It lets the code skip the bounds check
It sorts the queue by distance automatically
cards.answer: Each cell is enqueued once, at its nearest distance
cards.explanation: dist != -1 doubles as the visited mark. Several cells of one level can reach the same neighbour; setting it on enqueue stops duplicates and keeps O(m * n).

incorrectOptionExplanations.Distances set at pop time would always b: They would still be correct; the cost is duplicate queue entries.
incorrectOptionExplanations.It sorts the queue by distance automatic: BFS order already gives non-decreasing distance; marking is about duplicates.

promptVariants: What is the time complexity of the canonical code?
Derive the running time of the multi-source BFS.
options: O(m * n * Z), Z the number of zeros
cards.explanation: Each cell is enqueued at most once (dist == -1 check) and does four constant-time neighbour checks.

incorrectOptionExplanations.O((m * n)^2): That is a separate BFS from every cell.
incorrectOptionExplanations.O(m * n * log(m * n)): No heap is used; a deque BFS has no log factor.
incorrectOptionExplanations.O(m * n * Z), Z the number of zeros: All zeros share one BFS, not one each.

promptVariants: The dist matrix and the queue together use O(___) space.
Space of the multi-source BFS: O(___).
cards.explanation: dist has m * n entries and the queue can hold a large fraction of the cells (e.g. all zeros at the start).
